title: THE LAST TIME SAMUEL SPOKE TO SAUL
paragraphs:
THE LAST TIME SAMUEL SPOKE TO SAUL
The terrifying tragedy of a man who kept asking God for direction after repeatedly refusing what God had already said—and the breathtaking difference between Saul’s darkness and the grace waiting for sinners in Jesus Christ.
There is something more frightening than hearing a hard word from God.
It is reaching the day when you desperately want another word...
and discovering that the real problem was never that God had failed to speak.
You had simply refused to obey what He had already said.
That is where Saul’s story becomes painfully personal.
Because Saul did not begin his story hiding in darkness, consulting a forbidden medium, terrified of tomorrow.
He began as Israel’s king.
Chosen.
Anointed.
Given opportunity.
Given responsibility.
Given the word of God.
And yet, by the time we reach one of the darkest nights recorded in Scripture, the king who once stood among God's people is walking through the night disguised as someone else.
That detail should haunt us.
Because sin rarely begins by making you look like the person you will eventually become.
It begins with one compromise you can explain.
One command you partially obey.
One conviction you postpone.
One excuse that sounds reasonable.
One moment when protecting your reputation matters more than surrendering your heart.
Then another.
Then another.

Until eventually you are hiding in clothes that are not yours, walking toward something you once knew was wrong, desperately searching for a voice because you would not listen when truth was standing directly in front of you.
Saul's collapse did not begin at Endor.
It began much earlier.
In 1 Samuel 15, God commanded Saul concerning Amalek. Saul went into battle, but instead of carrying out the command as given, he spared King Agag and kept the best livestock.
Then Samuel confronted him.
Saul initially insisted:
“I have performed the commandment of the LORD.”
But Samuel could hear the evidence of Saul's disobedience.
The sheep were still bleating.
The cattle were still making noise.
Imagine the scene.
Saul is declaring obedience while the evidence of his compromise is making noise behind him.
And perhaps that is where this story stops being ancient history.
What is bleating behind your confession?
What have you renamed so you do not have to repent of it?
What are you defending that God has been asking you to surrender?
We can become astonishingly skilled at calling partial obedience faithfulness.
We can worship publicly while resisting God privately.
We can post Scripture and still protect secret sin.
We can know Christian vocabulary, attend church, pray emotional prayers, sing with tears in our eyes—and still negotiate with commands God never invited us to negotiate.
Samuel tells Saul something devastating:
“Behold, to obey is better than sacrifice.”
The Hebrew places enormous weight on hearing.
שְׁמֹעַ — shemōaʿ

It comes from שָׁמַע — shamaʿ, a Hebrew verb meaning to hear, listen, or heed. In biblical thought, genuinely hearing God is not merely receiving sound. It carries the idea of responding to what has been heard.
That is exactly where Saul kept collapsing.
He could hear Samuel.
He could speak about the LORD.
He could offer religious explanations.
But hearing that never becomes obedience is spiritually dangerous.
Samuel continued:
כִּי חַטַּאת־קֶסֶם מֶרִי
“For rebellion is as the sin of divination…”
The irony becomes almost unbearable when you know where Saul's story is going.
Samuel warns him that rebellion is like divination.
Later, Saul literally seeks forbidden divination.
The thing Samuel used as a comparison eventually became Saul's behavior.
Sin has a terrifying way of taking us farther than the first compromise seemed capable of going.
Saul eventually admits:
“I have sinned.”
But even there, Scripture exposes something deeper.
He tells Samuel that he feared the people and obeyed their voice.
Then, after admitting his sin, Saul asks Samuel to honor him before the elders and before Israel.
Do you see the tragedy?
He is losing a kingdom...
and he is still thinking about appearances.
He needs repentance.
But reputation remains in the room.
That is one of the most dangerous conditions of the religious heart: being more devastated that people might discover what you did than devastated that your sin offended God.
There is a kind of sorrow that wants consequences removed without wanting the heart transformed.
There is confession that says, “I was wrong.”
And there is repentance that says, “Jesus, I cannot keep protecting the thing that is destroying me.”
They are not always the same.
Samuel turns away.
Saul grabs the edge of Samuel's robe.
It tears.
And Samuel tells him that the LORD has torn the kingdom from him and given it to another.
Then comes one of the saddest sentences in Saul's story.
Samuel went to Ramah.
Saul went home.
And 1 Samuel 15:35 tells us that Samuel did not see Saul again until the day of Samuel's death. Samuel nevertheless mourned for Saul.
Think about that.
The prophet grieved for the king who would not listen.
Samuel was not celebrating Saul's destruction.
Truth can pronounce judgment and still grieve.
Biblical confrontation is not cruelty.
Sometimes the person warning you most seriously is the person refusing to pretend that the cliff in front of you is a harmless road.
Then Samuel dies.
Israel mourns him.
And time moves forward.
Until the night comes.
The Philistines gather for war.
Saul sees their army.
Scripture says he is afraid and that his heart trembles greatly.
He asks the LORD what to do.
But no answer comes through dreams.
No answer through the Urim.
No answer through the prophets.
And Saul says something in 1 Samuel 28:15 that may be among the loneliest confessions in Scripture:
צַר־לִי מְאֹד
Tsar-li me'od.
“I am greatly distressed.”
Then:
וֵאלֹהִים סָר מֵעָלַי
“God has departed from me.”
Read that slowly.
God has departed from me.
This is a man who once had Samuel speaking into his life.
A man who had been anointed.
A man who had received divine instruction.
Now he is terrified, desperate, and looking for guidance.
And here is the terrible irony:
Saul wants a new answer from God while standing under judgment for refusing God's previous answer.
Sometimes we ask, “God, why aren't You telling me what to do?”
when perhaps another question deserves to be asked:
“What was the last thing God clearly told me in Scripture that I have been refusing to obey?”
Not every season of divine silence means judgment. Scripture gives us faithful sufferers who cried to God through seasons when He seemed silent.
So we must not turn Saul's experience into a cruel formula and tell every hurting Christian that God's apparent silence proves secret rebellion.
It does not.
But Saul's particular silence cannot be separated from Saul's persistent rejection of God's revealed command.
And instead of allowing that silence to drive him toward humble repentance, Saul reaches for another source.
He asks his servants to find a בַּעֲלַת־אוֹב — baʿalat-ʾov, a woman associated with consulting the dead or a spirit-medium.
This is especially disturbing because Saul himself had previously removed mediums and spiritists from the land. Scripture explicitly reminds us of that fact before describing what happens next.
The king who enforced the prohibition is now secretly breaking it.
And then Scripture gives us a cinematic detail that almost preaches by itself:
וַיִּתְחַפֵּשׂ שָׁאוּל
“Saul disguised himself.”
He changed his clothes.
And went out at night.
There are moments when the outward action becomes a picture of the inward condition.
Saul has spent so long protecting appearances that now the king himself disappears underneath a disguise.
That is what hidden sin does.
Eventually you are not only hiding what you do.
You start hiding who you are.
There is the church version of you.
The Facebook version.
The family version.
The private version.
The version everybody praises.
And then the version sitting alone after midnight with the thoughts nobody knows about.
Maybe your darkness is not a medium at Endor.
Maybe it is pornography you keep deleting from your history but not from your life.
Maybe bitterness.
An affair.
A secret conversation.
A dishonest business practice.
A relationship you know is pulling you away from Christ.
Maybe pride wearing ministry clothing.
Maybe resentment toward God.
Maybe an addiction to approval.
Maybe you have learned how to look spiritually alive while privately becoming exhausted from maintaining the disguise.
Saul arrives at the woman's house at night and asks her to bring up Samuel.

The narrative then identifies the figure as Samuel. The woman sees Samuel and cries out; Saul himself does not initially see the figure but asks what she sees. Whatever questions readers may debate about the precise mechanics of this extraordinary event, Scripture never presents Saul's occult consultation as acceptable or as a technique believers may imitate. The entire episode is part of his tragic rebellion.
Then comes the voice Saul once had access to while Samuel was alive.
Samuel speaks.
But there is no new strategy.
No secret escape route.
No loophole.
Samuel essentially repeats what Saul had already been told.
“Why then do you ask me, since the LORD has departed from you…?”
Samuel reminds him that the kingdom has been taken and given to David.
And then Samuel reaches backward into Saul's history:
“Because you did not obey the voice of the LORD…”
There it is again.
The issue was not lack of information.
It was disobedience.
Saul crossed into forbidden darkness looking for a new answer...
only to hear the old answer again.

And this time, Samuel tells him that tomorrow Saul and his sons will die and Israel will fall into Philistine hands. The Hebrew narrative records Saul immediately collapsing full-length on the ground, terrified by Samuel's words.
Imagine the silence after that sentence.
A king on the floor.
A crown that suddenly means nothing.
Tomorrow is coming.
And Saul cannot command it to stop.
This is the last recorded conversation between Samuel and Saul.
No triumphant reconciliation.
No restored throne.
No second coronation.
Only the terrible harvest of years spent resisting the voice of God.
And if this article ended here, it would leave us in the darkness with Saul.
But the Bible does not end in 1 Samuel 28.
And your story does not have to end where Saul's did.
Because another King came.
Saul was Israel's failed king.
Jesus Christ is the faithful King.
Saul grasped at a kingdom he was losing.
Jesus possessed all authority and yet humbled Himself.
Saul repeatedly protected himself.
Jesus gave Himself.
Saul feared people.
Jesus perfectly obeyed His Father.
Saul's disobedience brought judgment.
Christ's obedience carried Him all the way to the cross, where He bore judgment for sinners.
This is where scandal meets grace.
Because Christianity does not announce that decent people can improve themselves enough for God to accept them.
The Gospel announces something infinitely better:
Christ came for sinners.
For rebels.
For hypocrites.
For people with histories.
For people who have worn disguises.
For people who knew better and still did it.
For people ashamed of what they became.
For people who cannot go backward and undo yesterday.
Jesus does not call your darkness light.
Grace never requires God to lie about your sin.
The cross proves how serious sin actually is.
But the cross also proves how far God's mercy was willing to go to save sinners.
Jesus died for sins and rose again.
And everyone who turns to Him in repentance and faith is not merely offered better religious advice.
There is forgiveness.
Reconciliation.
A new heart.
A new identity.
A new Lord.
A new future.
The scandal is what sin made of us.
The grace is what Jesus can make of a surrendered sinner.
Maybe you have been reading Saul's story and recognizing pieces of yourself.
Do not make the mistake of merely feeling emotional.
Conviction is mercy when it drives you to Christ.
You are reading this now.
You can confess now.
You can stop defending it now.
You can bring the secret into God's light now.
You can turn from the sin you have been feeding.
You can call upon Jesus Christ.
Do not wait until consequences force you to care about what conviction has been whispering for years.
Do not confuse God's patience with God's approval.
Do not keep asking Him to bless what His Word tells you to abandon.
And do not tell yourself you need to become clean enough before approaching Christ.
You come because you cannot cleanse yourself.
Come honestly.
“Jesus, I sinned.”
“Jesus, I have been hiding.”
“Jesus, forgive me.”
“Jesus, I surrender.”
“Jesus, save me and change me.”
That prayer is not a magic formula. Salvation rests in Jesus Christ, not in perfectly arranged sentences.
But call upon Him sincerely.
Turn to Him.
Trust Him.
Because the answer to Saul's tragedy is not “try harder to be Saul on his best day.”
The answer is Christ.
Maybe that is why this story hurts so deeply.
Some people will read it and remember the first conviction they ignored.
Some will remember the relationship God told them to leave.
Some will remember the apology they still have not made.
Some will remember the secret they promised God they would surrender.
Some will realize that they have been sacrificing religious activity while withholding obedience.
And someone reading this may finally realize:
“I have been asking God for another word while resisting the Word He has already given me.”
But if you are ready to stop hiding, you can simply write:
And if grace has been rebuilding places in you that sin once destroyed, leave a testimony:
“Christ is still healing me.”
Someone reading beneath you may need to know they are not the only person fighting their way back toward the light.
Not because sharing a Facebook post earns favor with God. It does not.
It cannot.
We glorify God through faith in Christ expressed in obedience, love, generosity, truth, worship, and lives surrendered to Him—not through transactions with a ministry.
But if this message is faithful to Scripture and helped you see Christ more clearly, sharing it can become one simple act of helping truth reach someone else.
Send it privately to the person you have been praying for.
One share can place the Gospel in front of someone you may never know was struggling.
There may come a night when you need to remember Saul's tragedy before making a decision that could become your own.

Supporting Gospel ministry financially is not a substitute for worship, obedience, generosity to your local church, or care for those in need. But voluntary support of faithful Christian teaching can be a meaningful form of partnership in spreading the Gospel.
Come to Jesus.
Because merchandise cannot redeem you.
A ministry cannot save you.
Only Christ can.
Saul's story leaves us with a question much more important than whether we found the story fascinating.
What will you do with the voice of God while you can still respond?
When Scripture exposes your pride—listen.
When Scripture confronts your sexual sin—listen.
When Christ commands forgiveness—listen.
When He calls you away from idolatry—listen.
When He exposes hypocrisy—listen.
When the Gospel tells you to repent and believe—listen.
Not because obedience purchases grace.
Because grace changes the people it saves.
Saul teaches us the horror of wanting God's guidance without wanting God's government.
Jesus offers something greater than guidance.
He offers Himself.
So stop protecting the disguise.
Stop negotiating with the conviction.
Stop rehearsing excuses.
Bring the scandal into the light.
Bring the failure.
Bring the secret.
Bring the shame.
Bring the years you wasted.
Bring the obedience you delayed.
Bring the pieces you cannot put back together.
Bring them to the crucified and risen Christ.
Because when Jesus takes hold of a surrendered life, your worst chapter does not have to become your final chapter.
And perhaps that is the line worth carrying with you long after you close this article:

Do not wait until you are desperate to hear God's voice before valuing the truth He has already spoken—and when your past tells you it is too late for redemption, run to Jesus while grace is calling your name.
